body: Berkshire 1986 letter (Scott Fetzer purchase-accounting appendix). Definition, verbatim: owner earnings are '(a) reported earnings plus (b) depreciation, depletion, amortization, and certain other non-cash charges ... less (c) the average annual amount of capitalized expenditures for plant and equipment, etc. that the business requires to fully maintain its long-term competitive position and its unit volume.' Add any extra working capital needed to hold position. Buffett admits (c) 'must be a guess' but says owner earnings, not GAAP, is 'the relevant item for valuation purposes', quoting Keynes: 'I would rather be vaguely right than precisely wrong.' Warning: Wall Street 'cash flow' = (a)+(b) without subtracting (c); 'you shouldn't add (b) without subtracting (c)'. When (c) exceeds (b), 'GAAP earnings overstate owner earnings' (his example: oil majors). Even See's spent $0.5-1m a year above depreciation 'simply to hold our ground competitively.' Closing line: 'accounting is but an aid to business thinking, never a substitute for it.' Actionable: for Indian capex-heavy firms (metals, telecom, airlines, cement), estimate maintenance capex from 5-10yr capex/depreciation history; treat EBITDA-based or 'cash-profit' pitches as red flags (the 2023 letter says 'EBITDA is a banned measurement at Berkshire').

data.formula: OE = net income + D&A + non-cash charges - maintenance capex - incremental WC to hold position

title: Buffett 1986: owner earnings = earnings + D&A - maintenance capex (not 'cash flow')

body: 1996 letter: 'Your goal as an investor should simply be to purchase, at a rational price, a part interest in an easily-understandable business whose earnings are virtually certain to be materially higher five, ten and twenty years from now. Over time, you will find only a few companies that meet these standards - so when you see one that qualifies, you should buy a meaningful amount of stock.' Also: 'If you aren't willing to own a stock for ten years, don't even think about owning it for ten minutes.' On competence: 'You only have to be able to evaluate companies within your circle of competence. The size of that circle is not very important; knowing its boundaries, however, is vital.' 1993: 'a policy of portfolio concentration may well decrease risk if it raises ... both the intensity with which an investor thinks about a business and the comfort-level he must feel with its economic characteristics', with risk defined 'as "the possibility of loss or injury"', not beta. But the same letter's other half: 'By periodically investing in an index fund ... the know-nothing investor can actually out-perform most investment professionals. Paradoxically, when "dumb" money acknowledges its limitations, it ceases to be dumb.' Concentration is only for the 'know-something investor' who can find 'five to ten sensibly-priced companies that possess important long-term competitive advantages.' 1988: 'our favorite holding period is forever' (for outstanding businesses + managements). Actionable: honest self-classification first; index core + concentrated satellite only in sectors where we have documented edge.
title: Buffett 1993/1996: circle of competence, concentration, and risk = possibility of loss

body: Scale (SEBI, data to 31 Jul 2026): 1,496 entities listed on SME platforms since inception (2012), 365 migrated to main board, Rs40,222 crore raised, combined market cap ~Rs4.71 lakh crore. Boom: FY24 was the record year with 196 SME IPOs raising >Rs6,000 crore; 159 more raised >Rs5,700 crore by 15 Oct 2024 (SEBI board memo, Dec 2024). Abuse documented by SEBI: IPO and rights proceeds 'diverted ... to related / connected parties or to shell companies controlled by promoters', and 'fraudulent sales and purchases through circular transactions amongst related parties' to create positive sentiment; SEBI issued an investor caution on 28 Aug 2024. Reforms approved Dec 2024 and notified in the ICDR amendment of March 2025: minimum application two lots and above Rs2 lakh (from ~Rs1 lakh); OFS capped at 20% of issue size and each seller can sell at most 20% of holding; operating profit of Rs1 crore in 2 of 3 preceding years (the Oct-2026 paper describes the existing test as EBIT); promoter lock-in for MPC raised to 5 years from 3; monitoring agency mandatory above Rs20 crore (from Rs100 crore); IPO only if issue size >Rs10 crore; 2-year cooling-off after conversion from partnership/LLP or change of control. Oct-2026 consultation paper proposes a Rs3 crore average operating profit test but also lowering the Rs2 lakh minimum application and aligning allocation with main board (RII category). Outcomes: tracker data show 58% of 2024 SME IPOs below issue (median -20%) (single-source). Actionable: treat SME listings as presumptively promoter-exit or manipulation vehicles unless cash-flow, auditor and related-party checks pass.

march_2025_rules.profit_test: Rs1cr operating profit in 2 of 3 yrs

data.oct_2026_proposal: avg op profit >=Rs3cr; lower min application

title: India SME IPO platform: boom, abuse and SEBI's 2025 reforms (and the Oct-2026 proposal to loosen some)

body: Agarwalla, Jacob and Varma, 'Four Factor Model in Indian Equities Market' (IIM Ahmedabad Working Paper 2013-09-05, revised Sep 2014; ~114 S2 citations) built Fama-French plus momentum factors for India from CMIE Prowess, Oct 1993-Dec 2013. Differences from earlier Indian studies: a wider firm universe, exclusion of illiquid stocks so portfolios are investible, a size cut-off suited to India's skewed size distribution, a correction for survivorship bias (many listed companies 'vanished'), and a 6-month gap for accounting data because AGMs are late. Results (average annual, arithmetic): momentum (WML) 21.9%, value (HML) 15.3%, size (SMB) about 0%, market risk premium 11.5%. Their monthly-updated data library is what our insight:iima-factor-premiums-india computed from, and the long-run picture is the same: 1994-2025 CAGR of WML 10.6%, HML 6.5%, SMB -3.8%. The gap between 21.9% arithmetic and 10.6% compounded is volatility drag plus the weaker 2014-25 decade, so quote CAGRs, not arithmetic means. Replicated: yes. The JKP global factor database independently includes India, and NSE momentum/value indices show the same signs, but momentum crashes (2000, 2009) and decade-long value droughts are real. Use for us: in India, momentum and value are documented premia and size is not, after excluding illiquid micro-caps. A 'small is beautiful' thesis needs a business reason, not a factor reason.
title: Agarwalla-Jacob-Varma (IIMA WP 2013/14): India momentum 21.9%/yr, value 15.3%/yr, size ~0 (arithmetic, 1994-2013), the source of the IIMA factor library

body: Own pre-registered backtest (run 2026-11-21; research_notes/Backtests/india_pead.md). Seeded random sample of 700 current NSE EQ/BE equities -> 580 usable companies, 10,026 quarterly-result events (train 2018-21: 4,336; test 2022-25: 5,690). SUE = seasonal random walk on standalone basic EPS (split-adjusted), (EPS_q - EPS_q-4) / sd of previous 4-8 seasonal changes; event = earliest NSE results announcement/broadcast timestamp; entry = close of first trading day strictly after it; quintiles within each fiscal quarter; inference across 16+16 quarters with 5,000-draw bootstrap. H1 (T-B, 63d): train +4.84% (CI +2.61 to +7.07, t 4.06), TEST +4.24% (CI +2.20 to +6.18, t 3.99) - passes t>3 in both periods and out of sample; 21d test +1.73% (t 3.9), 126d test +6.18% (t 3.5). H2 (top quintile vs median-116 size-matched controls, 63d): train +1.81% (t 2.1), test +2.36% (CI +0.94 to +3.67, t 3.23); net 0.5% round trip +1.86% (CI +0.44 to +3.17); net 1% +1.36% (CI -0.06 to +2.67) -> fails pre-committed rule 2 by a hair, so NOT labelled an edge candidate (126d clears 1% cost: +2.69%, CI +0.61 to +4.73, but 126d was not primary). Bottom quintile is the stronger leg: -2.70%/-2.13% vs controls at 63d (t -4.4/-4.8). Quintile ladder monotone (test Q1..Q5 -2.13, -0.80, +0.17, +1.02, +2.36%). Controls calibrated (all events vs controls ~0). H3 (bigger in smallest mcap tertile) NOT supported: small-minus-large test -0.44% (CI -4.8 to +3.8); exploratory: middle tertile (median Rs 2,800-3,600 cr) strongest in both periods (test 63d T-B +5.9%, t 4.6). Announcement-window T-B +3.75%/+4.95% (t 9/18) confirms dating. Revenue SUE weaker (test 63d T-B +2.1%, t 1.9). Skew: top-quintile event-level median excess -1.0% vs all-event median -2.6% (mechanical vs equal-weight controls); median and winsorised T-B still +3.2%/+4.1%; random 10-name baskets fall below 1% cost 21% of the time, 30-name 3%. Exploratory: long-only effect in test only in >= Rs 1,000 cr (+2.74%, t 3.9) vs < Rs 1,000 cr +0.36%; top-SUE with positive announcement reaction +3.32% (t 4.0). 2025 63d T-B only +0.9% (possible decay or noise). Survivorship: 253 of 1,508 (16.8%) Q3FY19 NSE filers are gone from today's list (failures + mergers); failures cluster in bottom SUE, so T-B likely understated. Lesson: PEAD survives in India (unlike US large/mid caps, Martineau 2022) - usable as an avoid-after-big-miss filter and a top-SUE research-queue tilt held 3-6 months in diversified baskets; not a multibagger engine.

survivorship.bias_direction: T-B likely understated; long-only roughly neutral

data.verdict: H1 supported (train and test, t~4); H2 supported gross, fails 1%-net CI rule by 0.06 pp -> not an edge candidate under rule 2 (borderline); H3 not supported

title: Backtest: post-earnings-announcement drift (PEAD) in Indian stocks (NSE Rs 500-50,000 cr, 2018-2025) - top-minus-bottom SUE quintile +4.2% over 63 trading days out of sample (t 4.0); long-only top quintile +2.4% vs size-matched controls gross, misses the 1%-cost rule by 0.06 pp
